label: D · Original C with teaching additions

sections.title: Human language and computation
Speech movements in MRI
Why speech is a remarkable learned skill

teaching.text: **Speech is one of the most complex skills a person ever learns, and almost nobody teaches it.** Children learn to move their speech organs in extremely complicated ways with no instructions and hardly any way to see what their tongue is doing. By the time they are two to four years old, they speak with a wide vocabulary and language that is close to an adult's.
children: Reading and writing whole words come later, around six or seven, and they need a great deal of explicit teaching.
So the skill that seems harder, speaking, is learned almost for free, while the skill that seems simpler, writing, has to be drilled.

teaching.text: The field that studies how the tongue, lips, velum and other parts of the vocal tract move is called **articulatory phonetics**. MRI images make these movements visible, even though a speaker can never watch them directly.
children: Voice assistants and other speech technology have recently come to imitate this human ability in ways almost nobody expected.
So the course studies speech twice, once as a human skill and once as something AI systems now model.

sections.title: Air vibration and acoustic phonetics

teaching.text: **Acoustic phonetics** studies the air inside the vocal tract and how that air vibrates. The air sits between the tongue and the rest of the vocal tract, and for the sake of understanding it, the curve of the tract can be ignored and the air pictured as a straight column.
children: The arrows on the MRI image straighten that bent passage out into a simple tube.
The vibration of the air in that tube is what turns the movements of the tongue and lips into the sounds a listener hears.

sections.title: Why scientific understanding of AI matters

teaching.text: **AI cannot simply be ignored, even though it causes real harm.** It has psychological, economic, social and environmental costs, and some scientists warn of even worse dangers, but it also has real benefits, such as helping with medical treatments. One of the biggest dangers is that **people know everything about how these systems are built and understand almost nothing about how they work.**
children: The number of people who actually know how these systems operate is very small.
So understanding AI matters for scientists who use it, for politicians who need to control it and for lawyers who argue about it.

teaching.text: The course exists because a creative thinker can help explain these systems well enough to gain their benefits while avoiding their harms.
children: That kind of understanding, rather than fear or blind use, is the goal.

sections.title: Course goals

teaching.text: The course has specific goals and general ones. The specific goals are to appreciate speech as a human cognitive skill, to understand basic principles of physics through speech, to understand how modern AI systems model human cognition, and to sharpen careful reasoning through elementary programming.
children: The general goal is to think creatively across fields, since the course draws on physics, psychology, linguistics, biology, economics, computer science and neuroscience.
It also aims to deepen understanding of the world people now live in and to make people more skillful users of modern AI.

sections.title: Moving from memorization to creative reasoning

teaching.text: **Diotima's ladder describes two very different ways of knowing.** At the bottom are daily experience, habit, memorization and repetition, where similar things are treated as the same and slightly different things are treated as different. At the top are creativity, insight, focus and imagination, where different things can turn out to be the same and similar things can turn out to be different. Each step up the ladder comes from asking a question and working out its answer.
children: For thousands of years, people could fake it and do well without ever climbing the ladder.
That is no longer possible, because job and graduate school interviews now look for exactly the abilities at the top of the ladder, such as posing problems, solving them and reading critically.

sections.title: Voicing and place through sustained fricatives

teaching.text: **Speech can be learned by doing it.** Saying a long f and then sliding into a v, a long th as in thing and then the th in that, a long s and then a z, and a long sh and then the sound in the middle of beige, makes the differences easy to feel.
children: Within each pair, the only thing that changes is whether the vocal folds vibrate, and that difference is called **voicing**.
Placing a hand on the throat makes it obvious, since the buzz switches on for v, z and the others and switches off for f, s and the others.

teaching.text: Moving from one pair to the next changes something else, which is **where in the mouth** the air is squeezed. That difference is called the **place of articulation**.
children: So each of these sounds is described by two separate choices, one about the vocal folds and one about where in the mouth the narrowing happens.

sections.title: The fricative system

teaching.text: **Fricatives** are sounds made by squeezing the air through a narrow gap, so that it becomes turbulent and hissy. They line up in a grid where one direction is the place of articulation and the other is voicing.
children: At the **labial** place the lower lip touches the upper teeth, giving f and v.
At the **dental** place the tongue tip is at the teeth, giving the two th sounds, and at the **alveolar** place the tongue is just behind the teeth on the ridge, giving s and z.
At the **postalveolar** place the tongue is a little farther back, giving sh and the sound in beige.

teaching.text: Each column of the grid has one voiceless sound and one voiced sound, so voicing and place combine freely.
children: The MRI images under each column let the place be identified by looking at where the tongue or lips make the narrowing.

sections.title: Stop place, voicing, and nasality

teaching.text: **Stops** are made by closing the vocal tract completely and then releasing the air. They come in three places, with p, b and m at the lips, t, d and n with the tongue tip at the alveolar ridge, and k, g and ng with the back of the tongue raised against the soft palate, which is the **velar** place.
children: In each row, the first sound is voiceless and the second is voiced, just like the fricatives.

teaching.text: The third sound in each row, m, n and ng, is a **nasal stop**. The mouth is closed just as for b, d or g, but the **velum** is lowered so that the air escapes through the nose.
children: So n and d share their place and their voicing, and they differ only in whether the air goes out through the nose or is blocked and then released through the mouth.
That gives three separate ways to tell consonants apart, which are voicing, place of articulation and the manner of letting the air out, with nasality as part of the manner.

lecture02.title: 02 · Speech structure and learning in AI

sections.title: Human language and technology
Lecture agenda
Internal coordination during speech
Fricative place and voicing

teaching.text: **Fricatives** squeeze the air through a narrow gap so that it hisses, and they are organized by two separate choices. One choice is the **place of articulation**, where the narrowing happens, which can be labial, dental, alveolar or postalveolar. The other choice is **voicing**, whether the vocal folds vibrate.
children: So f and v share the labial place and differ only in voicing, and the same holds for s and z, and for sh and the sound in beige.
Feeling the throat while sliding from one sound of a pair to the other makes the voicing difference easy to notice.

sections.title: Oral and nasal stop comparisons

teaching.text: **Stops** close the vocal tract completely and then let the air go. They are made at three places, the lips for p, b and m, the alveolar ridge for t, d and n, and the soft palate, the velar place, for k, g and ng.
children: In each row the first stop is voiceless and the second is voiced.
The third one is nasal, because the velum is lowered and the air escapes through the nose while the mouth stays closed.

sections.title: Three dimensions of consonant knowledge

teaching.text: **English consonants have far more structure than anyone notices when speaking.** Putting fricatives and stops into one table reveals three dimensions, which are voicing, place of articulation and **manner of articulation**, meaning how the air is let out.
children: Fricatives let the air through a narrow gap, **oral stops**, also called plosives, block the air completely and then release it through the mouth, and **nasal stops** block the mouth while the air goes out through the nose.
Nasal stops in English are always voiced.

teaching.text: Every consonant sits at one place in this table, so each one is described by a choice of voicing, a choice of place and a choice of manner.
children: For example, n and d are both voiced and both alveolar, and they differ only because n is a nasal stop while d is an oral stop.
Speakers use all of this structure without ever having been taught it, which says a lot about how much they already know.

sections.title: AI as a model of psychological abilities

teaching.text: **AI is a model of several psychological skills that animals have**, namely knowing, recognizing, attending, acting and learning. How AI models each of these skills is at least partly based on how humans do them.
children: So AI did not come out of nowhere as a purely technical invention.
Each piece of an AI system can be traced back to an idea about how minds and brains work.

sections.title: Taylor’s cloze procedure

teaching.text: **The question of how AI knows anything starts with a test called the cloze procedure.** It was invented as a way of measuring how readable a piece of writing is, by deleting words and asking readers to fill them in.
children: The name comes from the word closure, the idea that people mentally close up gaps in something that is almost complete.

sections.title: Closure turns incomplete input into a whole pattern

teaching.text: **Closure is a principle from Gestalt psychology.** In the figure of three broken circles, people see a whole triangle even though no triangle is drawn, because the mind fills in what is missing. The cloze procedure applies the same principle to language.
children: Given chickens cackle and blank quack, almost anyone fills in ducks right away.
Filling that gap correctly requires knowing the meanings of the words, how they combine and the structure of the whole sentence.

sections.title: What successful completion requires

teaching.text: **For AI, knowledge simply is the ability to complete a sequence.** A person's knowledge of a skill can be tested by asking them to finish some sequence, and AI takes this idea all the way, treating completion as all that knowing is.
children: If a system can reliably fill in the missing piece, it is treated as knowing the pattern.
Another word for completion is prediction, and people already predict and expect what comes next all the time.

sections.title: From words to vectors and next-word probabilities

teaching.text: **GPT works by taking in a bunch of words and predicting the next one.** To a computer, each word starts out as a list of random numbers, and the only requirement is that different words get different lists. A list of numbers like this is called a **vector**.
children: Given chickens cackle and ducks blank, a system that knows English gives back one long vector with a probability for every word of English being the next word.
That output is a **probability distribution**, so a word like quack should get a high probability while a word like cat or Zulu should get almost none.

sections.title: Weights carry the system’s learned knowledge

teaching.text: **The system turns the input vectors into the probability distribution by computing, and the computing is mostly plain grade school arithmetic.** It adds, subtracts, multiplies and divides.
children: The knowledge that turns the input numbers into the output probabilities is stored in another set of numbers called **weights**.
Today's AI systems have an enormous number of these weights, which is where everything they know is kept.

sections.title: Weights and synapses as a scale comparison

teaching.text: Having so many weights can seem too strange to resemble human knowledge, but human knowledge is stored in a similar way. Knowing that chickens cackle while ducks quack is stored in the **synapses**, the connections between the neurons of the brain.
children: The brain has an enormous number of synapses, even more than the weights of today's AI systems.
So a huge store of connection strengths is exactly where a brain keeps its knowledge too.

sections.title: Completion is a form of prediction

teaching.text: The idea that knowledge is completion can sound nonsensical at first. The best test is personal experience, by asking whether talking with an AI system feels like talking with something whose knowledge is totally different from one's own.
children: Whatever the system's notion of knowledge is, it does not seem totally different from a human one.
Calling completion **prediction** makes the idea feel more natural, since people constantly predict and expect what will happen next.

sections.title: Mistakes provide a direction for learning

teaching.text: **One of the most central issues in AI is how it learns, and it learns by making mistakes.** People may not be so different, since much of what people learn comes from their mistakes rather than from theory or practice alone.
children: The main learning algorithm of AI is called **stochastic gradient descent**.
It sounds intimidating, but it can be understood through a very easy example, which is finding an average.

sections.title: Averaging as observation-based error learning

teaching.text: Averaging a short list of numbers is easy, by just adding them up and dividing. But that direct method does not work for complex things like speech, language, biological molecules or scenes, which are the kinds of things AI deals with. So a different averaging method is built that learns from the data a little at a time.
children: It starts with a wild guess about the average, then looks at one number from the list and moves the guess a bit closer to that number.
Then it repeats with another number, which is called **observation-based error learning**.

sections.title: The correction rule of stochastic gradient descent

teaching.text: **Stochastic gradient descent finds the essence of a list of numbers by improving a guess step by step.** It begins with a random guess as the first estimate of the average. It then picks one number from the data at random, and the difference between the current guess and that number is the mistake, which is called the **loss**.
children: The guess is improved by subtracting a small fraction of the loss, so that it moves a little toward the number it just saw.
Then another number is picked at random and the same thing happens again, over and over.

teaching.text: The name says what the algorithm does. **Stochastic** means random, because the data points are picked randomly, **gradient** refers to the loss, and **descent** means reducing it.
children: So the whole algorithm is two ideas, which are making an initial guess and then using the data to improve that guess.

sections.title: Learning rate changes both speed and variability

teaching.text: Running the algorithm from three very different starting guesses, one too high, one about right and one too low, reveals how the **learning rate** matters. The learning rate is the fraction of the loss subtracted at each step.
children: With a small learning rate, all three guesses creep toward the true average slowly but smoothly and end up very close to it.
With a large learning rate, all three jump to the right neighborhood almost at once, but then they keep bouncing around it noisily and never settle.

teaching.text: So no matter where the guess starts, the algorithm finds the average. The starting guess only changes the path, while the learning rate changes how fast and how precisely it gets there.

sections.title: The speed–accuracy tradeoff

teaching.text: **Learning has a fundamental tradeoff between speed and accuracy.** Raising the learning rate makes learning faster but less accurate, and lowering it makes learning more accurate but slower.
children: There is no setting that gives both at once, which is the disappointing part.
Generations of people have made their living by finding better ways to optimize, so that learning becomes faster and more accurate at the same time.

sections.title: Dynamical systems 1
Lecture agenda
Elements, relations, and a goal

teaching.text: **Every dynamical system can be described by three things**, which are its **elements**, the **relations** between those elements, and the **goal** the whole system is working toward.
children: This simple lens works for animals, for people, for machines and for learning algorithms alike.
Asking what the parts are, how they affect each other and what the system is trying to reach is the first step in understanding any of them.

sections.title: An octopus coordinates its body with its environment

teaching.text: An **octopus** defending its den is a dynamical system. Its elements are its eight arms and the ground it pushes against. The relations between each arm, the ground and an approaching fish are planned by a nervous system that sits partly in its head and partly in the rest of its body.
children: The goal of the whole system is to keep its den.
All of the arms working together toward that one goal is what makes the behavior a single system rather than eight separate movements.

sections.title: Speech is an organized dynamical system

teaching.text: **Speaking is also a dynamical system.** Its elements are the many parts of the tongue, the lips, the velum, the larynx, the palate and the back wall of the throat, and the brain plans the relations between all of them.
children: The goal of the whole system is to convey a thought to a listener.
Just like the octopus arms, these parts have to be coordinated so that they all serve that one goal at the same time.

sections.title: Shared organization across very different systems

teaching.text: **People are full of dynamical systems.** Every voluntary action, and every involuntary action of the heart, the pancreas and the neurons, is a dynamical system, and its elements can be as big as organs or as small as cells and the chemicals inside them. Biology, chemistry and physics are all about dynamical systems, and the speech system is a very complex one.
children: Because dynamical systems are everywhere, one system can be used to study another, since they share an underlying similarity despite looking extremely different.
Seeing that very different things can be the same in this deep way is exactly the kind of thinking found at the top of Diotima's ladder.

sections.title: Motor primitives combine into a complex octopus action

teaching.text: The octopus example comes from real research analyzing a complex octopus action as a combination of simpler movement pieces. Studying how the octopus coordinates its arms to slap at a fish teaches something general about how a complex body achieves a goal.
children: The same way of thinking carries straight over to the tongue, which is also a flexible, muscular structure with no bones.
So studying one animal's dynamical system can shed light on how human speech is controlled.

sections.title: Knowledge and other psychological skills in AI

teaching.text: **AI is a model of several animal psychological skills**, which are knowing, recognizing, attending, acting and learning. The cloze procedure links these skills to language, because filling in a missing word is a test of knowing.
children: So the AI side of the course and the human side are studying the same abilities from two directions.

sections.title: Inputs, knowledge, and a predicted distribution

teaching.text: **In GPT, each word is a vector, a list of thousands of numbers**, and these input vectors are called x's or **tokens**. The system's knowledge about language is held in an enormous set of numbers called **weights**, or W's. The system mostly adds, subtracts, multiplies and divides to combine its weights with the vectors it is given.
children: The result of those calculations is a probability distribution that amounts to the system's guess for the next word.
How the weights combine with the input vectors is itself a dynamical system, but learning is an easier dynamical system to understand first.

sections.title: How initially random weights become useful

teaching.text: **The weights start out completely random, so the system begins by faking it until it makes it.** The system is given a sequence such as chickens cackle and ducks, and it predicts the next word by combining its random weights with the input vectors. Since the next word should be quack, the system is told to change its weights so that its output looks more like the right answer.
children: This is repeated with more and more sequences, billions of times, and each time the weights change a little to improve the guess.
That is how large language models both learn and come to know things.

sections.title: Random initialization and learning from mistakes

teaching.text: **AI learning rests on two tricks, faking it until you make it and learning by making mistakes.** The system starts out knowing nothing, with random weights, so at first it is just faking it.
children: Each wrong guess gets feedback, and the weights change a little so that the next guess is better.
After a huge number of these corrections, the system ends up with the right knowledge, which means it has made it.

sections.title: A simple model of learning an average

teaching.text: Averaging a short list is easy by adding the numbers and dividing, but that direct method does not carry over to speech, language, molecules or scenes. So a learning method is built instead, which makes a wild guess about the average and then improves it by looking at the data.
children: It looks at one number from the list, compares it with the current guess, and moves the guess a bit closer to that number.
Then it repeats with another number, which is called **observation-based error learning**.

sections.title: Start from an arbitrary estimate

teaching.text: **Stochastic gradient descent starts with a wild guess.** The goal is to find the average, which is the essence of a list of numbers, but the algorithm begins by picking any random number as its first estimate. Here the first guess is far above the real average on purpose.
children: The **learning rate** is set to one quarter, which means each step will move the guess a quarter of the way toward the number it is compared with.

sections.title: An observation exposes a discrepancy

teaching.text: **One observation creates an error.** A number is picked at random from the data and compared with the current guess, since the average ought to be close to the data. The difference between the guess and that data point is the mistake, which is called the **discrepancy** or the **loss**.
children: Here the guess is well above the data point, so the loss is positive.

sections.title: Correct a fraction rather than replacing the guess

teaching.text: **The guess then moves a quarter of the way toward the observation.** A quarter of the loss is subtracted from the current guess, and because the loss was positive, subtracting it pulls the guess down toward the data point.
children: The new guess is still too high, but it is closer than before.

sections.title: Correction after observation 2

teaching.text: **The same correction is repeated with a new random observation.** Another number is drawn from the data, the loss is found again, and a quarter of it is subtracted from the guess.
children: Since the guess is still above the new data point, the guess moves down again.

sections.title: Correction after observation 3

teaching.text: Each repetition follows the same recipe of comparing, finding the loss and moving a quarter of the way. As long as the guess sits above the data points it sees, every step pulls it lower.
children: The steps are not all the same size, because each one depends on how far the guess is from that particular data point.

sections.title: Correction after observation 4

teaching.text: After a few more corrections, the guess has come down a long way from its starting point. It is getting close to the region where the real data actually lies.
children: Each step still moves it only part of the way, so it approaches the average gradually rather than jumping there.

sections.title: A high observation pulls the estimate upward

teaching.text: **A high data point pulls the guess upward.** This time the randomly chosen number is above the current guess, so the loss comes out negative. Subtracting a negative amount actually adds to the guess, so the guess moves up toward that data point.
children: This is the purpose of the minus sign in the update, since it moves the guess toward the data point whether that point is above or below the guess.

sections.title: Correction after observation 6

teaching.text: With the next observation, which is lower again, the guess moves back down. So the guess is now being pushed from both sides, by data points above it and data points below it.
children: Being pulled in both directions is what keeps it hovering near the middle of the data.

sections.title: Correction after observation 7

teaching.text: The corrections keep coming, each one smaller when the guess happens to be near the data point and larger when it is far away.
children: The guess is now in the right neighborhood, and the remaining steps mostly fine-tune it.

sections.title: Correction after observation 8

teaching.text: Another low data point pulls the guess down a little further. Over many steps, the high and low observations balance each other out.
children: That balance point is exactly the average of the data.

sections.title: A high observation pulls the estimate upward

teaching.text: Once again a data point above the guess produces a negative loss, and the minus sign turns that into a step upward.
children: So the guess never runs away in one direction, because any data point on the other side of the guess pulls it back.

sections.title: Correction after observation 10

teaching.text: When a data point happens to be very close to the guess, the loss is tiny, so the guess barely moves.
children: This is how the method naturally slows down once the guess is good, since nearby data produce only small corrections.

sections.title: Correction after observation 11

teaching.text: The guess keeps jittering by small amounts as new random data points arrive.
children: Each step moves it toward whichever number was drawn, so its path is a little uneven.

sections.title: Correction after observation 12

teaching.text: After a dozen corrections, the guess has come down from its wild starting value to sit right around the true average of the list.
children: No division of a total was ever done, since the guess got there only by learning from its mistakes one observation at a time.

sections.title: Why the learning path jitters

teaching.text: **That is stochastic gradient descent**, and it has just two steps, which are making an initial guess and then using data to improve it. **Stochastic** means each observation is picked at random, **gradient** means the direction of the change comes from the loss, and **descent** means the mistake keeps getting smaller.
children: The path jitters because the observations are random, but its overall tendency is always toward the average.

sections.title: An estimate can fall while its loss falls

teaching.text: **As the estimate comes down toward the average, the loss comes down too.** With a second list of numbers and the same learning rate, a guess that starts far above the average falls toward it smoothly. The loss, measured as half the squared distance between the guess and the average, drops quickly toward zero at the same time.
children: Squaring the distance makes the loss positive whether the guess is too high or too low.

sections.title: An estimate can rise while its loss falls

teaching.text: **Starting below the average, the estimate rises while the loss still falls.** With the same data and the same learning rate, only the starting guess changes, and now the guess climbs up toward the average instead of falling.
children: The distance from the average still shrinks, so the loss still drops toward zero.
So the direction the guess moves can change, but the learning itself does not, because the mistake always gets smaller.

sections.title: Learning rate and starting condition

teaching.text: Running the algorithm from a high start, a start near the average and a low start, all three guesses end up at the same average. The **learning rate** decides how they get there.
children: With a small learning rate, the guesses creep in slowly and smoothly and settle very precisely.
With a large learning rate, they jump into the right neighborhood almost at once but then keep bouncing around it and never settle down.

sections.title: The learning tradeoff

teaching.text: **Learning faces a fundamental tradeoff between speed and accuracy.** A higher learning rate makes learning faster but less accurate, while a lower learning rate makes it more accurate but slower.
children: No single setting gives both, which is frustrating.
Generations of people have built careers on finding better ways to optimize, so that learning can be both fast and accurate at once.

lecture04.title: 04 · Dynamic programming and shared physical principles

sections.title: Dynamical systems 1
Lecture agenda
A staged shortest-path problem

teaching.text: **The shortest path problem asks for the cheapest way to get from a starting point to an ending point through a network of stages.** Here the start is A, the end is J, and in between are several stages of states, such as B and C, then D, E and F, then G, H and I. Each arrow between two states has a cost, and the total cost of a path is the sum of the costs along it.
children: The goal is to find the path from A to J whose total cost is the smallest.
Problems like this appear everywhere, from finding a driving route to deciding which sequence of sounds best matches a stretch of speech.

sections.title: Why the locally cheapest choice can lose

teaching.text: **The greedy algorithm always takes the cheapest next step without looking ahead.** Starting from A, it picks whichever arrow costs the least, then from that state it again picks the cheapest arrow, and so on until it reaches J. It is very fast, because it only ever compares the few arrows leaving the current state.
children: The trouble is that a cheap step early on can lead into a part of the network where a very expensive step waits later.
So greed is not good here, because the greedy path can end up far from the best one.

sections.title: Blank source page
Exhaustive search trades speed for certainty

teaching.text: **The exhaustive algorithm tries every possible path and adds up the cost of each one.** Because it checks everything, it is guaranteed to find the true shortest path, so it is very accurate.
children: But when there are many stages and many states, the number of possible paths explodes, so it takes a very long time.
The paths also overlap, sharing many of the same pieces, so the exhaustive algorithm keeps redoing the same additions over and over.

sections.title: Bellman’s decomposition

teaching.text: **Dynamic programming starts from Bellman's idea of imagining that part of the problem is already solved.** Suppose the best cost from B to J and the best cost from C to J were already known, and call them the values of B and C. Then the best cost from A to J would simply be the smaller of two sums, the cost of going from A to B plus the value of B, or the cost of going from A to C plus the value of C.
children: So the value of a state is the minimum, over all its next states, of the cost to get there plus the value already known at that state.

sections.title: Solve the smaller problems that supply the values

teaching.text: The catch is that the values of B and C are not actually known yet. Bellman's answer is to break a problem into subproblems that can be solved, and if those cannot be solved yet, to break them down further.
children: So the big question about A turns into smaller questions about B and C.
This is the heart of **dynamic programming**, which is solving a problem by decomposing it into smaller problems.

sections.title: Propagating known costs backward

teaching.text: The best cost from B to J is not known either, but it could be found if the best costs from D, E and F to J were known. And those could be found from the best costs of G, H and I to J.
children: At the last stage, the problem becomes trivial, because the value of G, H or I is just the cost of the single arrow from that state to J.
So the values are filled in starting at the end and moving backward toward A, one stage at a time.

sections.title: Choose the best total after calculating values

teaching.text: **After all the values are calculated it becomes safe to be greedy.** To find the actual best path, the algorithm starts at A and at each state simply moves to the next state with the best combination of step cost and value.
children: The key is to be greedy on the values, not on the raw costs.
The values already include everything that lies ahead, so following them leads straight along the shortest path.

sections.title: A value summarizes the relevant future

teaching.text: **Dynamic programming gives the algorithm foresight about the future.** In the original problem, a large cost late in the network can trap an early greedy decision that looked cheap at the moment. The values contain the future, because each value already includes every obstacle between that state and the end.
children: So decisions made on the values are the best decisions in the present, since the whole future from each state is wrapped up in its value.
This matches the philosopher's line that life can only be understood backwards but must be lived forwards, since the values are computed backward and then the path is walked forward.

sections.title: Recursive breakdown and reconstruction

teaching.text: **Dynamic programming begins by posing a problem, its subproblems, their subproblems and so on.** The big problem is solved by solving the subproblems, which in turn are solved by solving smaller subproblems. This continues until the problems are trivial to solve.
children: Then the solutions are carried back up to solve the bigger problems that contain them, all the way to the original problem.

sections.title: The rule for propagating a value

teaching.text: **The values are carried back from each stage to the stage before it by Bellman's idea.** The value at one state is the smallest of a set of numbers, and each of those numbers is the cost to one of the next states plus the value already found at that state.
children: Doing this once for each state, from the last stage back to the first, gives every value with no repeated work.
That is why dynamic programming is far more efficient than the exhaustive algorithm, since each overlapping piece is solved only once and then reused for every path that passes through it.

sections.title: Least distance and least time can diverge

teaching.text: **The best route can require taking a bad step early in order to avoid a much worse step later.** Dynamic programming may choose an expensive first arrow because it leads onto a route that never gets stuck at the costly step further on. It can seem as if planning like that needs a big brain.
children: But nature solves the same kind of problem without thinking.

A lifeguard reaching a swimmer on a uniform beach just runs straight, but when the swimmer is in the water, the fastest route runs farther along the sand, where running is fast, and then cuts into the water, where swimming is slow.

sections.title: Refraction shares the least-time principle

teaching.text: **Decision-making turns out to work just like physics.** Light does the same thing as the lifeguard when it passes from air into water, bending so that it takes the path of least time, which is why a pencil in a glass of water looks bent.
children: So choosing a bad stretch early to avoid a worse one later is not something only a planning brain does.
The same principle of finding the best overall path appears in physical systems, in decision-making and in dynamic programming.

sections.title: Reading the completed state values

teaching.text: **Working the values out on the network reveals the best route.** Each state gets written next to it the best cost from there to J, starting with G, H and I and moving back through D, E and F, then B and C, and finally A.
children: Once every state has its value, the best route is found by walking forward from A and always stepping to the state that the values point to.
The route found this way can start with an arrow that greedy would have rejected, because it avoids a costly step later on.

sections.title: Pop quiz heading
Learning and coffee share approach to equilibrium

teaching.text: **Learning and cooling follow the same kind of curve.** The guess of stochastic gradient descent, starting from very different points, approaches the true average quickly at first and then more and more slowly. A cup of hot coffee cooling down, or iced coffee warming up, approaches room temperature in exactly the same way.
children: In both cases the change is fast when the system is far from its goal and slow when it is close.
So a learning algorithm and a cooling drink are the same kind of dynamical system, each one moving toward an equilibrium.

sections.title: Dynamical Systems 3
Homework reminder
Position and velocity change each other

teaching.text: **A harmonic oscillator is built from two elements, x and v, that change each other.** The interest is in how x and v change over time because of how they are related. A dot over a letter, which is Newton's way of writing it, stands for how fast that quantity is changing as time goes on.
children: When the change of a quantity is positive, the quantity rises, and when its change is negative, the quantity falls.
The two rules of the oscillator are that the change of x equals v, and that the change of v equals the negative of x.

sections.title: Read the sign of the change

teaching.text: An example makes the two rules concrete. If v is negative, then the change of x is negative, so x goes down.
children: If x is negative, then the change of v is the negative of a negative, which is positive, so v goes up.
So each element pushes on the other, and neither one ever stays still for long.

sections.title: Two different sign relationships

teaching.text: **Reading the two rules in words is what makes the oscillator easy to follow.** The first rule says that whenever v is positive x rises, and whenever v is negative x falls. The second rule says that whenever x is positive v falls, and whenever x is negative v rises.
children: So x is always being pushed by v, while v is always being pushed back against x.
That back-and-forth pushing is exactly what makes the system swing.

sections.title: Follow the position–velocity cycle

teaching.text: **Following the x and v system through time reveals an oscillation.** When x starts out negative and v starts at zero, the second rule makes v rise, and once v is positive, the first rule makes x rise toward zero. When x reaches zero, v is at its largest, so x keeps going and overshoots into positive values, and now the second rule pulls v back down.
children: Once v becomes negative, x starts falling again, and the whole cycle repeats.
So x traces a smooth wave that goes up and down forever, and v traces the same kind of wave, shifted so that it peaks whenever x is passing through zero.

sections.title: A closed feedback loop

teaching.text: **The oscillation comes from a loop between two elements.** x drives the change of v, and v drives the change of x, so each one keeps feeding the other.
children: This is the simplest picture of a vibrating dynamical system.
It is the same story as a mass on a spring, where the position drives the spring's push and the motion carries the mass past equilibrium.

sections.title: Homework reminder
Harmonic oscillators across systems

teaching.text: **Almost everything can be treated as a harmonic oscillator, if one is brave enough.** Vibrations appear in the air of the vocal tract, in the vocal folds, in the economy, in music and even in the matter everything is made of.
children: Recognizing one shared pattern in such different places is the creative leap the course keeps asking for.

sections.title: Compression and rarefaction of air

teaching.text: **A slice of air in the vocal tract is also an oscillator.** Where the bits of air are squeezed very close together, the pressure is high, and where they are spread far apart, the pressure is low.
children: As a sound passes through, the air at each spot keeps swinging between being squeezed together and being spread apart.
So the air in the mouth is doing exactly what x does in the x and v system.

sections.title: Connect air motion to a cosine

teaching.text: **There is a cosine in your mouth.** The pressure of the air inside the vocal tract rises and falls over time in the same smooth wave that the x and v system produces.
children: That wave is the shape of a cosine, which is the signature of a harmonic oscillator.
But in each vowel, the air does not vibrate at just one frequency, because several of these waves are present at once.

sections.title: Vowels depend on tongue position

teaching.text: **Vowels differ in the shape of the vocal tract, and two dimensions describe them.** One dimension is **height**, how high the tongue is, which ranges from high to low. The other is **backness**, how far forward the tongue is, which ranges from front through central to back.
children: Dean is high and front, while Dune is high and back, with the lips rounded as well.
Dan is low and front, Don is low and back, and Done sits in the central region.

sections.title: Vowels combine more than one vibration
Praat demonstration
Two vibrating parts of speech

teaching.text: **Two different things vibrate during speech.** One is the air in the vocal tract, whose pressure swings like a cosine, and the other is the pair of vocal folds in the larynx.
children: The vocal folds open and close very quickly, and their vibration is what gives voicing its buzz.
So speech involves one vibrating system driving another, with the vocal folds setting the air in the tract into vibration.

sections.title: Economic cycles around a growth trend

teaching.text: **The economy also behaves like a harmonic oscillator.** The business cycle swings through peaks and troughs, from recession to recovery and back again, around an overall trend of growth.
children: Each swing overshoots the trend in one direction and then comes back and overshoots in the other, just as x does.
So the same mathematics that describes air in the mouth also describes booms and busts.

sections.title: Meadows reading reminder
Music and vibration

teaching.text: **Music is all about harmonic oscillators.** Every note comes from something vibrating, such as a string, a column of air in a wind instrument or the skin of a drum.
children: The written score is a set of instructions for which vibrations to produce and when.

sections.title: Atoms, shell pictures and wave modes

teaching.text: **Even matter is made of oscillators.** Atoms contain electrons that behave like vibrations, some at low frequencies and some at high frequencies, and physicists describe them with a version of the harmonic oscillator.
children: So the people studying the air in the mouth and the people studying atoms are using the same basic idea.
That is the strongest sense in which almost everything is a harmonic oscillator.

sections.title: Python position–velocity demonstration

teaching.text: **The x and v system can also be run in Python.** A short program starts x and v at some values and repeatedly applies the two rules, a little at a time, to move both forward through time.
children: Plotting x over time from such a program produces the same up and down wave as the reasoning in words.
Programming the system is a way of checking the reasoning, since the computer only follows the two rules and nothing else.

sections.title: Dynamical Systems 5
Two quantities in an oscillator

teaching.text: **The harmonic oscillator is a loop of two quantities, x and v, that keep changing each other.** The change of x over time equals v, so v drives x. The change of v over time equals the negative of x, so x drives v, but in the opposite direction.
children: The dot over a letter means how much that quantity increases or decreases as time goes on.
When x is high, v is pushed down, and when v is negative, x falls, so the two keep chasing each other around the loop.

sections.title: Repeated change in a loop

teaching.text: **This loop is the basic dynamical system behind every oscillation, or vibration.** Each variable pushes on the other, so there is no single cause at the start and no single effect at the end.
children: Whenever x reaches the middle, v is at its largest and carries x past it, and whenever v reaches zero, x is at its farthest point and turns v around.
So the system never comes to rest on its own, and it keeps swinging back and forth.

sections.title: Why a spring and a mass make vibration

teaching.text: **Vibration needs two physical effects working together**, a spring and a mass. The **spring** is the springiness found in many things, and its strength is called its **stiffness**. The **mass** is what carries motion once something is moving.
children: Vibration is what is felt when a car hits a bump, it is music, it is the boom and bust of the economy, and it is the bouncing estimate of stochastic gradient descent with a high learning rate.
It is also the motion of the air in the vocal tract and of the vocal folds during speech.

sections.title: Air particles move closer and farther apart

teaching.text: **A slice of air in the vocal tract behaves like a spring and a mass.** Where the bits of air are squeezed close together the pressure is high, and where they are spread far apart the pressure is low.
children: Squeezed air pushes back to spread out again, which is its springiness, and moving air keeps moving, which is its mass.
So the air in the mouth has both ingredients that vibration needs.

sections.title: Balancing feedback reduces displacement

teaching.text: **A spring by itself gives what is called negative or balancing feedback.** In a system where the change of x is a negative fraction of x, a positive x makes x fall and a negative x makes x rise. Starting from a positive value, x falls by a fraction of its current size, then by a fraction of the smaller size, and so on, so it drifts toward zero more and more slowly.
children: Starting from a negative value, it rises toward zero in the same gradual way.
These are systems that move only in order to reach their **equilibrium**, the natural resting position, and the size of that fraction is the stiffness, so a stiffer spring gets there faster.

sections.title: Mass carries motion onward

teaching.text: **A mass that is moving just keeps on moving.** A car traveling at a constant velocity covers the same distance every moment, without anything pushing it forward.
children: This is the idea of inertia, worked out by Galileo, Descartes and Newton, that a mass in motion stays in motion.
So mass is the opposite kind of effect from a spring, since a spring wants to stop at a place while a mass wants to keep going.

sections.title: Returning to a place versus passing through it

teaching.text: **A spring stops at a place, while a mass stops only after a process.** A spring with no mass, pulled away from its natural position, simply moves back and stops right at that position. Once a mass is attached, the mass reaches the natural position while it is still moving, so it keeps going and overshoots.
children: The spring then pulls it back, and it overshoots again in the other direction.
That combination of a spring that wants to go back and a mass that wants to keep moving is exactly what produces vibration.

sections.title: Air expansion follows a cosine

teaching.text: **There is a cosine in the mouth.** The air pressure at a spot inside the vocal tract rises and falls in the smooth wave of a cosine, which is the same wave the x and v loop produces.
children: But in a vowel the air does not vibrate at a single frequency.
Several of these waves happen at the same time, and together they make up the sound of the vowel.

sections.title: Compare tongue configurations for vowels

teaching.text: **Vowels are described by tongue height and tongue backness.** High vowels like the ones in dean and dune have the tongue raised, and low vowels like the ones in Dan and Don have it lowered. Front vowels like dean and Dan have the tongue pushed forward, while back vowels like dune and Don have it pulled back, with done in the central region.
children: So dean and dune are both high vowels, and they differ because dean is front while dune is back, with the lips rounded as well.
Changing the shape of the tract in these ways changes how the air inside it vibrates.

sections.title: Frequency counts cycles in a fixed interval
Different combinations give different vowel patterns
Predict the effect of mass and stiffness

teaching.text: **Perturbation theory asks what happens to the frequency of a mass-spring system when one of its parts is changed.** If the mass is increased, the frequency decreases, because a heavier mass is harder to turn around. If the stiffness is increased, the frequency increases, because a stiffer spring pulls back harder.
children: So raising the mass makes the system vibrate more slowly, and raising the stiffness makes it vibrate more quickly.
These two rules are the basis for understanding how hearing and speech work.

sections.title: Hearing separates a mixture into frequencies

teaching.text: **Hearing is explained by the two perturbation rules.** Inside the ear, the **basilar membrane** is heavy and not very stiff at one end, and light and very stiff at the other end.
children: Since frequency goes down with mass and up with stiffness, the heavy, loose end vibrates at low frequencies and the light, stiff end vibrates at high frequencies.
Each part of the membrane is connected to neurons, so the brain can tell which frequencies were heard from where along the membrane the vibration happened.

sections.title: Learning rate trades speed for steadiness

teaching.text: **Learning faces the same tradeoff between speed and accuracy.** A higher learning rate makes learning faster but less accurate, and a lower learning rate makes it more accurate but slower.
children: With a high learning rate, the estimate keeps bouncing around the right answer, which is the oscillation of stochastic gradient descent.
Raising the stiffness of a spring and raising the learning rate both make the system reach its goal faster.

sections.title: Dynamical Systems 6
Exam reminder
A spring alone and a mass–spring system

teaching.text: **A spring stops at a place, but a mass-spring system stops only after a process.** A spring with no mass, pulled away from its natural position, goes straight back to that position and stays there. Once a mass is attached, the mass arrives at the natural position while it is still moving, so it keeps going, overshoots and stretches or squishes the spring on the other side.
children: The spring then pulls it back, it overshoots again, and the cycle repeats.
So the spring supplies the goal of going back to equilibrium, and the mass supplies the motion that carries it past that goal, and together they vibrate.

sections.title: Mass, stiffness and the frequencies of speech

teaching.text: **Perturbation theory says that raising the mass lowers the frequency and raising the stiffness raises it.** A heavier mass is harder to turn around, so the system vibrates more slowly, while a stiffer spring pulls back harder, so it vibrates more quickly. When people speak, they change the effective mass and stiffness of different portions of air in the vocal tract, differently for each vowel and consonant.
children: So when the air is set vibrating by the vocal folds, it vibrates at many frequencies at once, and which frequencies they are depends on where and how much the air is squeezed.

For a listener to understand speech, the ear has to work out which low, middle and high frequencies are present, so that the brain can tell, for example, that one set of frequencies means scene while another set means son.

sections.title: The cochlea connects incoming sound to neural signals

teaching.text: **Sound reaches the brain through the ear.** Waves of vibration in the air arrive at the outer ear and travel inward to the inner ear, to a coiled part called the **cochlea**. The cochlea is the part that sends signals to the brain about which frequencies are in the sound.
children: The many other names of the parts of the ear do not need to be memorized, but the cochlea does.

sections.title: The path into the basilar membrane

teaching.text: **Inside the cochlea is the basilar membrane.** Sound vibrations pass from the eardrum through three tiny bones into the coiled cochlea, and running along the inside of that coil is a long membrane called the **basilar membrane**.
children: Uncoiled, the membrane would be a long strip, and its properties change gradually from one end to the other.
That gradual change along its length is the key to how the ear separates frequencies.

sections.title: Frequency is represented by place and nerve activity

teaching.text: **Hearing is explained by mass and stiffness changing along the basilar membrane.** One end of the membrane is heavy and not very stiff, while the other end is light and very stiff. Since frequency goes down with mass and up with stiffness, the heavy, loose end vibrates at low frequencies and the light, stiff end vibrates at high frequencies, with the frequencies in between laid out along the membrane.
children: Each part of the membrane is hooked up to neurons that send signals to the brain.
So the brain knows which frequencies were heard from where along the membrane the vibration happened, and this discovery won a Nobel Prize.

sections.title: How vocal folds make and change pitch

teaching.text: **The vocal folds are a mass-spring system that speakers can tune.** They are small muscles in the larynx, and like all muscle they have mass and stiffness, so other muscles attached to the surrounding cartilage can stretch them to make them stiffer or bunch them up to make them effectively heavier.
children: Stiffer folds vibrate faster and heavier folds vibrate slower, so this control lets people sing, signal questions, mistrust, belief, surprise and emotion in English, and change the meanings of words in tone languages.
The rate at which the vocal folds vibrate is called **pitch**, or **F0**, the fundamental frequency.

teaching.text: **The vocal folds vibrate because of air pressure and suction.** When air is taken into the lungs and the vocal folds are closed, pressure builds up beneath them until it blows them apart, and air flows between them.
children: Just like a shower curtain being pulled inward, the flowing air sucks the folds back together, and then the pressure below blows them apart again.
This repeats many times per second, and the suction is the same **Bernoulli force** that lifts airplanes.

sections.title: Position-first updates keep the oscillator bounded

teaching.text: **The harmonic oscillator can be solved step by step with simple arithmetic.** Starting with x at its high point and v at zero, each step uses the current v to nudge x forward a little, and then uses the new x to nudge v forward a little. Repeating this over and over builds up two lists of numbers, one for x and one for v.
children: Plotted over time, x falls from its high point through zero to a low point and climbs back, while v dips negative and comes back up, a quarter of a cycle out of step.
So a few lines of adding and multiplying trace out the same vibration that the reasoning in words predicts.

sections.title: Explicit Euler uses the old pair for both updates

teaching.text: **The order of the updates matters.** In the explicit version, both new values are computed from the previous pair of x and v, rather than updating x first and then using the new x for v. With the same step size, the swings of x and v in this version grow larger and larger with every cycle.
children: That growth is not something a real spring would do, because it is an error caused by the method and the size of the step.
Taking smaller steps makes the error smaller, which is one more version of the tradeoff between speed and accuracy.

sections.title: Arithmetic can approximate continuous change

teaching.text: **Euler's explicit method solves differential equations using nothing but arithmetic.** Each new value is the old value plus its rate of change multiplied by a small time step.
children: Rules about how things change over time can therefore be turned into a simple repeated calculation that a person or a computer can carry out.
Calculations like this, done by hand, were once used to plan real space flights, and the same idea runs inside the computers that simulate speech, weather and much more.

sections.title: Python demonstration
Software 1.0
Neural Networks 1
Exam reminder
Differential equations express how systems change

teaching.text: **Differential equations are the mathematical way of writing down dynamical systems.** A differential equation states how a quantity changes over time, given its current state, just as the rules of the x and v system do. Newton first hid this idea in a coded message, and it can be paraphrased as saying that the laws of nature are expressed by differential equations.
children: So spring systems, cooling coffee, the air in the vocal tract and learning algorithms can all be written in the same kind of mathematics.
Both inference and learning in large language models are differential equations too.

sections.title: Predict a return toward equilibrium step by step

teaching.text: **A viscous spring gives negative, or balancing, feedback, and Euler's method predicts what it will do.** In a system where the change of x is minus one third of x, a starting value well above zero falls by a third of itself in the first step. The following step takes away a third of that smaller value, so the drop is smaller, and each later step is smaller still.
children: So x moves toward zero quickly at first and then more and more slowly, without ever overshooting.
Finding x at each moment this way, by plugging the current value back into the rule again and again, is **Euler's method**, which predicts what the world will do using only arithmetic.

sections.title: Blank source page
